fields.questionText: Two cells of 3 V each are connected in parallel. An external resistance of 0.5 Ω is connected in series to the junction of two parallel resistors of 4 Ω and 2 Ω, and then to the common terminal of the battery through each resistor, as shown in the figure. What is the current flowing through the 4 Ω resistor?
solutionSteps: [1 mark] Two identical 3 V cells in parallel give an emf of 3 V. 4 Ω ∥ 2 Ω = (4×2)/(4+2) = 4/3 Ω; total R = 0.5 + 4/3 = 11/6 Ω; I = 3 ÷ (11/6) = 18/11 ≈ 1.64 A. Current through 4 Ω = I × 2/(4+2) = 6/11 ≈ 0.55 A. Correct option (b) 0.55 A.

fields.questionText: The current flowing through a wire of resistance 2 Ω varies with time as shown in the given figure (the vertical axis shows the current in ampere; each of the three segments lasts 1 s). The amount of heat produced (in J) in 3 s would be
solutionSteps: [1 mark] H = I²Rt for each 1 s interval: 3²×2×1 = 18 J; (−2)²×2×1 = 8 J; 1²×2×1 = 2 J. Total H = 18 + 8 + 2 = 28 J (the sign of the current does not matter as I² is used). Correct option (c) 28 J.

fields.questionText: The given figure shows the filament in a lamp. The filament is made from a very thin piece of metal. When there is a current in the filament it glows brightly and becomes very hot. Explain how the current causes the filament to become hot.
fields.answer: The filament has resistance which opposes the flow of charge; the moving electrons do work against this resistance (colliding with the metal ions), so electrical energy is converted into heat energy (H = I²Rt), and the very thin filament becomes hot enough to glow.
fields.finalAnswer: The filament has resistance which opposes the flow of charge; the moving electrons do work against this resistance (colliding with the metal ions), so electrical energy is converted into heat energy (H = I²Rt), and the very thin filament becomes hot enough to glow.
solutionSteps: [1 mark] The metal of the filament has resistance, which opposes the flow of charge (electrons).
[1 mark] The moving electrons do work against this resistance — they collide with the ions of the metal, transferring energy to them.
[1 mark] So electrical energy is converted into heat (thermal) energy (Joule heating, H = I²Rt); the thin filament gets very hot and glows.

solved_answer: Resistance of filament ⇒ electrons do work against it (collisions with ions) ⇒ electrical energy → heat (H = I²Rt), filament glows
rationale: Figure is a bulb with labelled filament — matches but illustrative. Single explain item with no case sub-parts: adopted fixer's re-tag to Section C 3-mark Short, keeping a figure reference ('The given figure') since the image is bound.
